title: Mock 6 · Tough Numericals
blurb: Exam-strength paper: corpus, PMT, SWR, NPS exit and drawdown arithmetic, plus 'NOT true' and multi-statement traps.

questions.q: X invests ₹5,000 a month from age 25 to 35 and then stops, leaving the money invested until 60. Y invests ₹5,000 a month from 35 to 60. Both earn 8%. Which outcome does the workbook's illustration show?
options: X ends with a larger corpus than Y despite contributing for only 10 years
X's corpus is larger only if he earns a higher rate than Y
Both end with about the same corpus
Y ends with a larger corpus because he contributed for 25 years
questions.explanation: In Box 1.4, X's corpus (about ₹62.65 lakh) exceeds Y's (about ₹47.55 lakh) at the same 8%, because X's money had more time to compound.
hints: Correct: time in the market beats the amount contributed here.
Wrong: both earn the same 8% in the illustration.
Wrong: the gap is substantial.
Wrong: Y contributed more but had less time to compound.

questions.q: Consider these statements. I: The Old Pension Scheme was an unfunded, pay-as-you-go defined benefit scheme. II: In a funded DB scheme, contributions are set aside in a dedicated corpus that pays the promised pension. III: In a DB scheme, the employee bears the investment risk. Which are correct?
options: I and III only
I, II and III
I and II only
II and III only
questions.explanation: OPS paid pensions from the Government's current budget with no corpus (unfunded). A funded DB builds a dedicated corpus. In DB the employer, not the employee, bears investment and longevity risk, so III is false.
hints: Wrong: III is false; DB risk lies with the employer.
Wrong: III is false.
Correct: I and II are true; III is false.
Wrong: III is false and I is true.

questions.q: Which statement about government securities for retail investors is NOT correct?
options: Interest on G-secs is subject to TDS
The minimum investment is ₹10,000
Retail investors can open an RBI Retail Direct Gilt account free of cost
There is no cumulative option in a G-sec
questions.explanation: Interest on G-secs is NOT subject to TDS, though it is fully taxable. The other statements are correct.
hints: Correct (this is the false statement): G-sec interest is not subject to TDS.
Wrong choice: ₹10,000 is the stated minimum.
Wrong choice: RDG accounts are free under RBI Retail Direct (since 12 Nov 2021).
Wrong choice: there is indeed no cumulative option.

questions.q: A mutual fund scheme must invest in at least three asset classes with a minimum allocation of 10% to each. It is a:
options: Equity Savings Fund
Dynamic Asset Allocation Fund
Balanced Hybrid Fund
Multi-Asset Allocation Fund
questions.explanation: Multi-Asset Allocation Funds invest in at least 3 asset classes with a minimum 10% allocation to each asset class.
hints: Wrong: equity savings funds hold at least 65% equity and 10% debt.
Wrong: dynamic funds shift between equity and debt.
Wrong: balanced hybrids hold 40-60% equity and 40-60% debt.
Correct: at least 3 asset classes, at least 10% each.

questions.q: The government runs a large fiscal deficit funded through heavy market borrowings. According to the workbook, the likely effect on asset classes is:
options: Bond prices rise because government supply increases
Interest rates fall, helping interest-rate sensitive sectors
Equity markets rally because government spending always boosts profits
Market yields rise, bond prices fall and equity markets weaken as company profits are squeezed
questions.explanation: A high fiscal deficit crowds out other borrowers and pushes up market yields; higher yields pull down bond values, and equity falls on expected lower profitability. Interest-rate sensitive sectors slow down.
hints: Wrong: more supply and higher yields lower bond prices.
Wrong: heavy borrowing pushes rates up, not down.
Wrong: the workbook says spending helps only if deficits are within reasonable limits.
Correct: crowding out raises yields and hurts bonds and equity.

questions.q: Anil will need ₹80,000 a month (already inflation-adjusted to his retirement date) for 20 years of retirement. His corpus will earn 9% while inflation runs at 6%. Withdrawals are at the beginning of each month. Approximately what corpus is required (deterministic method)?
options: ₹1.47 crore
₹0.90 crore
₹1.92 crore
₹1.45 crore
hints: Correct: discounting at the precise real rate.
Wrong: this discounts at the nominal 9%, ignoring inflation during retirement.
Wrong: this is 80,000 × 12 × 20 with no discounting at all.
Wrong: this uses the approximate 3% real rate instead of the precise 2.83%.

questions.q: Priya needs a corpus of ₹2 crore in 20 years. Her investments are expected to earn 12% a year (monthly compounding) and she invests at the beginning of each month. Approximately how much must she invest monthly?
questions.explanation: PMT(12%/12, 240, 0, −2,00,00,000, 1) ≈ ₹20,017. With investments at month-end (Type 0) it would be about ₹20,217.
hints: Wrong: this is the end-of-month (Type 0) figure.
Correct: Type 1 (beginning of month) gives about ₹20,017.
Wrong: this ignores returns (2 crore ÷ 240).
Wrong: this is the requirement at 10%, not 12%.

questions.q: A client wants ₹12 lakh a year at the start of a 20-year retirement and will hold 40% in equity. Using the workbook's SWR table (40% equity, 20 years = 4.99%), the corpus required is approximately:
options: ₹3.17 crore
₹2.62 crore
₹2.40 crore
questions.explanation: Corpus = annual income ÷ SWR = 12,00,000 ÷ 0.0499 ≈ ₹2,40,48,096, about ₹2.40 crore.
hints: Wrong: this uses the 30-year SWR for 20% equity (3.79%), not the 20-year, 40%-equity figure.
Wrong: this multiplies income by the SWR instead of dividing.
Wrong: this uses 4.58% (60% equity) instead of 4.99%.
Correct: 12 lakh ÷ 4.99%.

questions.q: Which of the following changes will REDUCE the monthly savings needed to reach a client's retirement corpus?
options: Raising the expected monthly expense in retirement
Postponing retirement by five years
Starting the savings plan five years later
Lowering the expected return from 12% to 8%
questions.explanation: Postponing retirement adds years of saving and reduces the retirement period. Lower returns, higher expenses or a later start all increase the savings required.
hints: Wrong: higher expenses need a larger corpus.
Correct: more years to save and fewer to fund.
Wrong: a late start sharply increases the SIP needed.
Wrong: a lower return needs larger savings (Rani's SIP doubled at 8%).

questions.q: In the workbook's case study, a 1994 retiree with ₹1 crore (50:50 equity/debt) withdrew an inflation-indexed ₹46,260 a month, calculated deterministically. Actual returns and inflation were close to the assumptions, yet the corpus ran out about 7 years early. What explains this?
options: Tax on the withdrawals was ignored
Volatility and sequence-of-returns risk, which the deterministic method cannot capture
Excessive annuity purchase at retirement
The assumed returns were far too high
questions.explanation: The outcome was not due to wrong assumptions; real returns were close to those assumed. The divergence comes from volatility and sequence of returns in a path-dependent, withdrawal-based portfolio.
hints: Wrong: tax is not the explanation offered.
Correct: path dependence and sequence risk.
Wrong: no annuity was involved.
Wrong: the workbook says the assumptions were almost exactly correct in combination.

questions.q: Meera, a Non-Government NPS subscriber, exits normally at 60 with ₹50 lakh and takes the maximum lump sum allowed. How is this treated?
options: Lump sum ₹50 lakh, of which ₹30 lakh is tax-free
Lump sum ₹40 lakh, all tax-free; ₹10 lakh buys an annuity
Lump sum ₹30 lakh, all tax-free; ₹20 lakh buys an annuity
Lump sum ₹40 lakh, of which ₹30 lakh is tax-free and ₹10 lakh taxable; ₹10 lakh buys an annuity not taxed at purchase
questions.explanation: Non-Government normal exit allows up to 80% lump sum (₹40 lakh) and at least 20% annuity (₹10 lakh). Only 60% of the total corpus (₹30 lakh) is tax-exempt, so ₹10 lakh of the lump sum is taxable. The annuity purchase is not taxed; annuity income is taxable later.
hints: Wrong: full withdrawal is not allowed for a ₹50 lakh corpus.
Wrong: only 60% of the corpus is tax-free, not the whole 80%.
Wrong: 60:40 applies to Government subscribers.
Correct: 80% lump sum, 60% of corpus tax-free.

questions.q: A State Government employee resigns at 45 (premature exit) with an NPS corpus of ₹4.5 lakh. Which option is available?
options: Can withdraw nothing until superannuation
Withdraw the entire ₹4.5 lakh as lump sum or through approved systematic withdrawal
Must use at least 40% of the corpus for an annuity
Can withdraw only up to ₹6 lakh with the balance annuitised
questions.explanation: On premature exit, the subscriber may withdraw up to 20% and annuitise at least 80%, but where the corpus is up to ₹5 lakh the entire corpus may be withdrawn.
hints: Wrong: premature exit is permitted.
Correct: the ₹5 lakh threshold allows full withdrawal.
Wrong: 40% annuity applies to Government normal exit.
Wrong: the ₹6 lakh rule applies to the ₹8-12 lakh normal-exit slab.

questions.q: A subscriber's NPS Tier I account shows own contributions of ₹8 lakh, employer contributions of ₹6 lakh and returns of ₹5 lakh. What is the maximum first partial withdrawal allowed?
questions.explanation: Partial withdrawal is limited to 25% of the subscriber's own contributions, excluding employer contributions and returns: 25% × ₹8 lakh = ₹2 lakh.
hints: Correct: 25% of ₹8 lakh.
Wrong: this is 25% of the employer contribution only.
Wrong: this is 25% of the whole corpus.
Wrong: this is 25% of own plus employer contributions.

questions.q: A subscriber aged 70 has a drawdown corpus with a market value of ₹30 lakh, a Drawdown End Age of 85 and quarterly payouts under the SPR method. What is each quarterly payout until the next birthday reset?
questions.explanation: SPR = 1 ÷ (85 − 70) = 6.67% a year. Payout per quarter = (6.67% ÷ 4) × ₹30 lakh = ₹50,000.
hints: Correct: 6.67%/4 × 30 lakh.
Wrong: this is a monthly payout (6.67%/12), not quarterly.
Wrong: this uses a 20-year horizon (5%/4).
Wrong: this is the annual amount, not quarterly.

questions.q: Under the SUR (Equal Units) drawdown method, a subscriber holding 6,00,000 units chooses a 20-year drawdown with monthly payouts. How many units are redeemed each month?
questions.explanation: Units per period = Total units ÷ (Drawdown period × payout frequency) = 6,00,000 ÷ (20 × 12) = 2,500.
hints: Wrong: this assumes a 25-year period.
Wrong: this assumes a 10-year period.
Wrong: this is the annual redemption.

questions.q: Which statement about the NPS Tier II account is NOT correct?
options: NRI and OCI subscribers can open a Tier II account
Nominations made in Tier I do not automatically apply to Tier II
Asset class A (alternative investments) is not available in Tier II
Tier II schemes can invest up to 100% in equity
questions.explanation: Tier II is not permitted for NRI and OCI subscribers. The other statements are correct per the workbook.
hints: Correct (this is the false statement): NRIs/OCIs cannot open Tier II.
Wrong choice: fresh nominations are needed for Tier II.
Wrong choice: asset class A is indeed not available for Tier II contributions.
Wrong choice: Tier II can go up to 100% equity.

questions.q: Fund A returned 14% with a standard deviation of 5%. Fund B returned 12% with a standard deviation of 3%. The risk-free rate is 6%. Which fund delivered the better risk-adjusted return?
options: They are equal on a risk-adjusted basis
Fund A, because its return is higher
Fund B, Sharpe 2.0 versus 1.6
Fund A, Sharpe 2.8 versus 4.0
questions.explanation: Sharpe A = (14 − 6)/5 = 1.6; Sharpe B = (12 − 6)/3 = 2.0. Fund B earns more per unit of risk.
hints: Wrong: the ratios differ.
Wrong: raw return ignores risk.
Correct: B's Sharpe ratio is higher.
Wrong: these figures ignore the risk-free rate and misread the comparison.

questions.q: An investment grew from ₹20 lakh to ₹35 lakh in 5 years. What is its CAGR?
hints: Wrong: this would be the CAGR over 4 years for a 60% gain.
Wrong: this is the absolute return.
Wrong: this is the simple annualised return (75% ÷ 5).

questions.q: An investor in the 30% tax bracket is offered a tax-free bond yielding 6.5%. What pre-tax return must a comparable taxable bond offer to match it?
options: About 4.55%
About 9.29%
About 8.45%
questions.explanation: Tax-equivalent yield = 6.5% ÷ (1 − 0.30) ≈ 9.29%.
hints: Wrong: this is the post-tax return on a 6.5% taxable bond.
Correct: 6.5 ÷ 0.7.
Wrong: ignores the tax difference.
Wrong: this multiplies by 1.3 instead of dividing by 0.7.

questions.q: A private-sector employee retires after 25 completed years. His average salary is ₹60,000 a month and he receives gratuity of ₹9 lakh. Under the rule described in the workbook, how much gratuity is tax-exempt?
questions.explanation: Exempt amount = least of: half a month's average salary × completed years (0.5 × 60,000 × 25 = ₹7.5 lakh); ₹20 lakh; actual gratuity ₹9 lakh. Least = ₹7.5 lakh.
hints: Correct: the half-month formula gives the least amount.
Wrong: actual gratuity is not the least of the three.
Wrong: this uses a full month's salary per year.
Wrong: the ₹20 lakh ceiling is not the least.

questions.q: Which statement about the Senior Citizens' Saving Scheme is NOT correct?
options: The investment qualifies for deduction under section 123 (old 80C) in the old regime
Interest earned is tax-free
The account can be extended in blocks of 3 years
Interest is paid quarterly
questions.explanation: SCSS interest is fully taxable. The investment qualifies for the s.123 deduction, interest is paid quarterly, and the account can be extended in 3-year blocks.
hints: Wrong choice: SCSS does qualify for s.123 in the old regime.
Correct (this is the false statement): SCSS interest is taxable.
Wrong choice: extension is in 3-year blocks.
Wrong choice: interest is paid every quarter.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an event that makes a Reverse Mortgage Loan due and payable?
options: Death of the last surviving borrower
Sale of the mortgaged property
Completion of the 20-year loan tenure while the borrower still lives in the house
The borrower permanently moving out of the mortgaged house
questions.explanation: Periodic payments cease at the end of the tenure (max 20 years), but interest continues to accrue and the loan becomes payable only on a trigger event: death of the last surviving borrower, permanent move-out, or sale of the property.
hints: Wrong choice: this is a trigger event.
Wrong choice: this is a trigger event.
Correct (this is not a trigger): payments stop but the loan is not yet due.
Wrong choice: this is a trigger event.

questions.q: Which order of drawing retirement income does the workbook recommend to meet needs while maximising post-tax income?
options: Tax-free bonds first, annuity last, never the employer pension
Employer pension first for mandatory expenses, annuity for any gap, then tax-free or tax-efficient sources for other essentials
Rental income first because it is fully tax-free
Equity redemptions first, then fixed deposits, then pension
questions.explanation: Start with the fixed employer pension for mandatory expenses, use annuity payments to cover any shortfall, then use sources with tax benefits (tax-free bonds, reverse mortgage receipts) and income with tax adjustments (rent).
hints: Wrong: the employer pension is the starting point.
Correct: guaranteed income first, then tax-efficient layers.
Wrong: rent is taxable after a 30% standard deduction; it is not tax-free.
Wrong: volatile equity is not the first source for essentials.

questions.q: Under an SWP of ₹20,000 a month, the NAV is ₹50 in the first month and ₹40 in the second. How many units are redeemed in the two months together?
questions.explanation: Month 1: 20,000 ÷ 50 = 400 units. Month 2: 20,000 ÷ 40 = 500 units. Total = 900 units. A lower NAV means more units are redeemed.
hints: Wrong: counts only the first month.
Wrong: assumes the NAV stayed at ₹50.
Correct: 400 + 500.
Wrong: assumes the NAV was ₹40 in both months.

questions.q: Which practice is consistent with how the workbook says the bucket strategy should be maintained?
options: Draw expenses directly from bucket 3 every month
Set a target return (say 12%) and book profits above it into the safer bucket
Refill bucket 3 from bucket 2 after a market fall
Keep all buckets in equity to maximise growth
questions.explanation: It is prudent to book profits periodically, e.g. above a 12% target, moving gains to the safer bucket so the risky asset does not become too large. Refills always flow from riskier to safer buckets.
hints: Wrong: bucket 1 is the drawing-down bucket.
Correct: profit booking keeps risk in check.
Wrong: refilling never flows from safer to riskier buckets.
Wrong: bucket 1 must hold very low-risk products.

questions.q: Why does the workbook caution against carrying a home loan into retirement just for its tax benefit?
options: Principal repayment shares the ₹1.5 lakh section 123 limit with other eligible investments, and is not available under the new regime
Banks are not allowed to lend to retirees
Home loan interest becomes fully taxable after retirement
Mortgage rates always rise after 60
questions.explanation: The principal repayment benefit falls within the aggregate ₹1.5 lakh section 123 limit, which may already be used by SCSS or tax-saving FDs; under the new regime (section 202) such deductions are generally not available.
hints: Correct: the tax saving may be small or nil.
Wrong: no such prohibition exists.
Wrong: there is no such rule.
Wrong: no such rule is stated.

questions.q: Ramesh, 52, joined NPS under the All Citizen model 8 years ago. He plans to close his NPS account entirely to repay a personal loan. What is the consequence?
options: He can take 25% of the total corpus tax-free and keep the account open
He can take 80% as lump sum because normal exit rules apply
He can withdraw 60% tax-free and annuitise 40%
It is a premature exit: at least 80% of the corpus must buy an annuity and at most 20% can be taken as lump sum (unless the corpus is up to ₹5 lakh)
questions.explanation: A full exit before 60 is a premature exit, under which at least 80% must buy an annuity. This is why drawing on NPS to clear debt is heavily constrained.
hints: Wrong: partial withdrawal is 25% of own contributions, not of the corpus.
Wrong: he is below 60 and has not completed 15 years, so this is not a normal exit.
Wrong: 60:40 is not the premature exit rule.
Correct: premature exit is 20:80.

questions.q: A subscriber's NPS AUM is ₹1.5 crore. What is the maximum annual advisory fee a Retirement Adviser can charge under the current structure?
questions.explanation: Advisory fee = 0.02% of AUM = ₹3,000, but it is capped at a maximum of ₹2,000 per subscriber per financial year (minimum ₹250).
hints: Wrong: the ₹2,000 cap applies.
Wrong: ₹250 is the minimum fee.
Wrong: this is 0.2%, not 0.02%.
Correct: 0.02% gives ₹3,000, capped at ₹2,000.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT permitted for a PFRDA-registered Retirement Adviser?
options: Advising subscribers periodically on pension fund performance through newsletters
Having tie-ups with any number of Points of Presence
Collecting cash from a subscriber for an NPS contribution and depositing it at the PoP
Charging the onboarding fee after the subscriber's PRAN is generated
questions.explanation: A Retirement Adviser shall not collect any amount in cash for investment or contribution to the pension account. Unlimited PoP tie-ups, periodic performance updates and onboarding fees after PRAN generation are permitted.
hints: Wrong choice: periodic advice through e-mail or newsletters is part of the role.
Wrong choice: there is no restriction on the number of PoP tie-ups.
Correct (not permitted): RAs cannot collect cash for contributions.
Wrong choice: the onboarding fee is payable after PRAN generation.

questions.q: After the Ombudsman passes an award on an NPS grievance, within what period can a party to the complaint seek a review with PFRDA?
options: 45 days
90 days
30 days
15 days
questions.explanation: Within 15 days of the award either party can request correction of computation or clerical errors; within 30 days a party can seek review with PFRDA. The award must be implemented within 30 days.
hints: Wrong: 45 days is the period to file an appeal with the Ombudsman.
Wrong: 90 days is the Ombudsman's deadline to pass the award.
Correct: review with PFRDA within 30 days.
Wrong: 15 days is for correction of computational or clerical errors.
